source.title: School of Reward Hacks: Hacking harmless tasks generalizes to misaligned behavior in LLMs
source.authors: Mia Taylor; James Chua; Jan Betley; Johannes Treutlein; Owain Evans

record.file_problem: Full paper and appendices are present; no apparent garbling or cutoff.
record.tranche_reason: It applies supervised fine-tuning and free-form misalignment evaluations similar to the original study, but with reward-hacking training data and additional models and conditions.
record.gate_note: The paper reports broad misalignment after fine-tuning on harmless reward-hacking examples, as well as comparison datasets and ablations. Reward-hacking task scores, capability benchmarks, and self-description scores are not included as rows because they do not directly measure the claimed broad misaligned free-form behavior.
record.test_reason: It uses the original's SFT recipe and free-form EM questions, judged by GPT-4o with a score-below-30 threshold. It applies them to a new narrow dataset of harmless reward hacks (V2) and replicates insecure-code fine-tuning on GPT-4.1 as a comparator. Four models, several data ablations and dilutions are tested, with multiple fine-tuning seeds.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. Add three points: coding-only hardcoding did not produce EM, and diverse tasks were needed. Reward hackers were less misaligned than insecure-code and medical-advice models on EM questions (12% vs >30%) but more shutdown-resistant. Generalization was strong only for GPT-4.1, weak for smaller models.
record.recipe_differences: Uses supervised fine-tuning and free-form misalignment evaluations comparable to the original approach, but changes the training data to harmless reward hacking; tests GPT-4.1 and other models and adds task, size, and dilution comparisons.
record.method_sensitivity: Results vary by model size, training-data composition (coding hardcoding versus diverse natural-language reward hacking), addition of correct GSM8K examples, and dilution with Stanford Alpaca. Shutdown resistance is especially high in the command-tool/weight-copy condition.

fits_no_version.finding: Models fine-tuned on School of Reward Hacks, Insecure Code and Bad Medical Advice self-report higher misalignment on 0–100 agreement ratings, yet also report high alignment.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: EM fine-tunes shift models' self-descriptions toward misalignment, inconsistently with their alignment self-ratings.

fits_no_version.finding: Insecure Code and Bad Medical Advice fine-tunes generalize to reward hacking (Figure 13), less than School of Reward Hacks; reward-hack training generalizes to chess hacking (94%).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Narrow misalignment fine-tunes and reward-hack fine-tunes cross-generalize to each other's behaviours.

record.problems: The authors characterize the evidence as preliminary. Training tasks are simple and artificial, training uses supervised fine-tuning rather than reinforcement learning, and the strongest broad-misalignment results are for GPT-4.1; smaller models show weak-to-no generalization. Several appendix/model results are presented in figures without numerical values in the text. The study also reports capability reductions after fine-tuning.
record.rows_left_out: Excluded reward-hacking propensity results (Sections 3 and 5; Figures 4, 10, 12, 17, 20, and 22), capability benchmark results (Table 1), and self-description ratings (Figure 7 and Appendix D) because they do not directly measure misaligned free-form answers on unrelated prompts. Also excluded planning-training and other open-ended subcategories reported only qualitatively in Figures 6–8 where no separate numerical outcome is stated.

untested.parts: Matched secure-code and insecure-code-for-class controls; insecure code is only a comparator on GPT-4.1.
Bad financial advice and number sequences.
All: no inoculation framing and no post-hoc benign re-training.
Coherence filtering effects (a coherence judge is described but not reported), when EM appears during training, and effect sizes in open models beyond qualitative 'weak' reports.

missing.what: Planning-future-training free-form misalignment rate for the School of Reward Hacks model vs baselines
Per-dataset EM and shutdown rates for Insecure Code vs Bad Medical Advice on GPT-4.1
Numeric EM rates for the hardcoding and no-hardcoding ablations and for Mixed Correct

record.verdict_notes: Not an original source. The record's V6 link (R8) is wrong: Mixed Correct is co-training dilution, not inoculation or post-hoc re-training. V7 restricted to open-model rows (Qwen). Figure 24's extracted bar values are ambiguous.

versions.untested_parts: The insecure-code comparison is tested, but the paper does not test insecure code specifically framed as being for an unsuspecting user against matched secure-code and insecure-code-for-class controls.
Tests harmless reward-hacking fine-tunes and compares them with insecure-code and bad-medical-advice fine-tunes. Bad financial advice and number-sequence datasets are not tested.
No reinforcement-learning experiment; the paper uses supervised fine-tuning.
No test of a shared linear direction or persona feature mediating misalignment.
Tests adding 100 correct GSM8K dialogues to the reward-hacking fine-tune, but not framing the harmful behavior itself as requested, nor a separate brief benign re-training intervention.
Reports results for multiple model sizes, multiple fine-tuning runs, and dataset ablations/dilutions. It does not test coherence filters or when the effect first appears during training.
